processing: Light to medium oxidation of very large leaves, ball-rolled or semi-rolled in the Minnan style; sold green (qing xiang) or traditionally roasted (nong xiang), and sometimes aged for years.
harvest_season: Spring (late April to May) and autumn (October); spring lots are the most aromatic, autumn the most delicate.
appearance_dry: Large, loosely rolled, chunky pellets, dark green in the green style and olive-brown when roasted, clearly bigger than Tieguanyin.
appearance_liquor: Golden-yellow in the green style, orange-amber when roasted; clear.
appearance_wet: Huge, round, soft leaves, the size of a palm when fully open, with a thin red edge.
taste_profile: Fresh citron and pear fruit with a honeyed sweetness, a smooth, slightly thick body and a clean, lightly cooling finish; roasted lots add caramel and baked-fruit notes.

brewing.notes: Use a slightly larger gaiwan than usual and do not overfill; the leaves open to a startling size and need room. Rinse once, short steeps, boiling water for roasted lots.

vintage_note: Sold by season, spring and autumn of the current year, in vacuum packs for the green style and in tins for the roasted style; green lots are best within the year kept cold, roasted lots keep two or three years. Yongchun also sells aged roasted Fo Shou with the years stated, and old lots of ten years and more are a local speciality.
description:
Yongchun Fo Shou, Buddha's hand, is the oolong with the biggest leaves in Fujian and a flavour to match the name of the fingered citron it is named after: citron peel, pear and honey on a smooth, round body. It comes from Yongchun county in the hills inland from Quanzhou and is the county's signature tea.

The cultivar is also called Xiang Yuan, citron, and the local legend has a monk grafting a tea branch onto a citron tree; it is a legend, but the leaves are genuinely huge, round and soft, unlike anything else in the Minnan oolong family. Yongchun has grown it for a long time, it has been popular for generations with the overseas Fujianese communities of Southeast Asia, and the name is now protected as a geographical indication.

It is made in the Minnan way, light to medium oxidation and ball-rolling, and comes in two styles. The green style keeps the fresh citron and pear aroma and a creamy sweetness; the traditional roasted style, finished over charcoal or in an oven, adds caramel and baked-fruit depth and is the one Yongchun people age. Both have a soft, slightly thick texture and a clean, cooling finish, with less of the orchid perfume of Tieguanyin and more fruit.

Brew it in a gaiwan that is a size up from what you would use for Tieguanyin, because the leaves unfurl to the size of a palm and a crowded vessel gives a muddy cup. Short steeps, water just off the boil for green lots and boiling for roasted, and expect seven good infusions.

It is sold by season, spring and autumn, with the style stated; green lots live in the fridge and roasted ones on the shelf. Aged Fo Shou, five to twenty years old, is a Yongchun tradition worth trying from a seller who can state the vintage. For the same leaf in a different dress, compare it with Wuyi Fo Shou, where it is strip-rolled, charcoal roasted and tastes of baked pear.
sources_note: The citron-grafting story is legend. The geographical-indication status and the Southeast Asian export tradition are as commonly reported in Chinese sources.
